power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=0.547", "p=0.150", "p=0.178"), Sentence = c("The cohorts did not differ significantly in age, sex distribution, or the scan-speech gap (age: t(160.2) = -0.60, p=0.547; sex: χ²(1) = 2.07, p=0.150; scan-speech gap: t(69.6) = 1.36, p=0.178).", "The cohorts did not differ significantly in age, sex distribution, or the scan-speech gap (age: t(160.2) = -0.60, p=0.547; sex: χ²(1) = 2.07, p=0.150; scan-speech gap: t(69.6) = 1.36, p=0.178).", "The cohorts did not differ significantly in age, sex distribution, or the scan-speech gap (age: t(160.2) = -0.60, p=0.547; sex: χ²(1) = 2.07, p=0.150; scan-speech gap: t(69.6) = 1.36, p=0.178)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Spontaneous language offers a scalable, non-invasive approach for identifying biological indicators of preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD).

We examined prediction of APOE4 carrier status and cerebral amyloid-β (Aβ) burden using Cookie Theft picture-descriptions from two cohorts, including Hebrew-and English-speakers (IRAP, N=134; and WRAP, N=1,541).
Aβ burden was classified across lowest-quartile, median, and highest-quartile cutoffs, capturing accumulation below conventional amyloid-positivity thresholds.

We compared embeddings from pretrained large language models (LLMs) to standard cognitive test scores, reflecting current clinical assessment, and theory-driven linguistic features, reflecting traditional language analysis.
Embedding-based models achieve the highest F1 among constituent models in five of eight tasks for APOE4 status and global Aβ.
High prediction disagreement suggests complementary signals between approaches.

An any-positive ensemble significantly outperforms every constituent model and a prior-informed random baseline across all eight tasks, and is also significantly superior to all constituent models in 21 of 24 regional Aβ tasks.

These findings highlight the complementarity of LLM-based, theory-driven, and cognitive measures for predicting AD-related genetic risk and pathology, and supports development of early screening approaches.
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder and the most common cause of dementia.
Its pathological processes can begin many years before clinically apparent symptoms, creating an important challenge for early detection and intervention.
Early identification is particularly important because available treatments and preventive measures are most effective before substantial cognitive deterioration has occurred [1] [2] [3] .
text.formatted: Early identification is particularly important because available treatments and preventive measures are most effective before substantial cognitive deterioration has occurred <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> .

text.text: However, current diagnostic pathways are often initiated only after symptoms become noticeable, when the underlying pathology may already have been developing for decades 4 .
text.formatted: However, current diagnostic pathways are often initiated only after symptoms become noticeable, when the underlying pathology may already have been developing for decades <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: This motivates the search for accessible, non-invasive methods that can identify signals associated with AD risk and pathology at early stages.
Language is a particularly promising source of information for this purpose.
Language production involves multiple cognitive processes, and changes in linguistic abilities have long been recognized as characteristic of AD progression.
Indeed, language-related tasks are central components of standard neuropsychological assessments, (e.g., verbal fluency, naming, and verbal memory tests [5] [6] [7] ).
text.formatted: Indeed, language-related tasks are central components of standard neuropsychological assessments, (e.g., verbal fluency, naming, and verbal memory tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> ).

text.text: Beyond these structured assessments, spontaneous speech provides an opportunity to examine how individuals produce language in a more naturalistic setting.
One widely used approach is the Cookie Theft picture-description task 8 , in which participants describe a standardized visual scene.
text.formatted: One widely used approach is the Cookie Theft picture-description task <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> , in which participants describe a standardized visual scene.

text.text: The simplicity of collecting such speech samples, together with advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), has motivated substantial research into languagebased indicators of cognitive impairment and dementia.
Earlier studies investigated linguistic changes through manual annotation and relatively simple quantitative measures [9] [10] [11] .
text.formatted: Earlier studies investigated linguistic changes through manual annotation and relatively simple quantitative measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> .

text.text: More recent work has employed Natural Language Processing (NLP) and machine learning to extract linguistic information automatically and predict cognitive status from speech.

These approaches include models based on predefined, theory-driven linguistic features, such as lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, and word frequency [12] [13] [14] [15] [16] [17] , as well as models that learn representations of language directly from data [18] [19] [20] [21] [22] [23] .
text.formatted: These approaches include models based on predefined, theory-driven linguistic features, such as lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, and word frequency <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> , as well as models that learn representations of language directly from data <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> .

text.text: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) has substantially expanded the possibilities for the latter approach.

Trained on very large text corpora to predict and generate language and perform a broad range of linguistic tasks, LLMs develop internal representations that capture rich aspects of linguistic meaning and context.
These representations offer a promising means of identifying subtle language patterns that may be difficult to specify in advance.
LLMs can also support automatic extraction of complex linguistic features that typically require human judgment, reducing the need for extensive manual annotation.
Despite this progress, an important scientific and clinical challenge remains.
Much of the research on language-based AD prediction studies have focused on distinguishing individuals with dementia or Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) from cognitively healthy controls 24 .
text.formatted: Much of the research on language-based AD prediction studies have focused on distinguishing individuals with dementia or Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) from cognitively healthy controls <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> .

text.text: Although these studies have established that language contains useful information about cognitive impairment, they leave open a more fundamental question: Can language provide information about AD-related biological risk and pathology before clear clinical symptoms emerge?
Addressing this question requires moving beyond the prediction of cognitive status toward biological indicators associated with the earliest stages of the disease.
In this work, we focus on two such indicators: apolipoprotein E ε4 (APOE4) carrier status and cerebral amyloid-β (Aβ) burden.
APOE4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for lateonset AD, with carriers facing an elevated risk of developing the disease 3, 25 .
text.formatted: APOE4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for lateonset AD, with carriers facing an elevated risk of developing the disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> .

text.text: Aβ accumulation, in turn, is a central feature of AD neuropathology and can begin long before the onset of overt cognitive impairment 26 .
text.formatted: Aβ accumulation, in turn, is a central feature of AD neuropathology and can begin long before the onset of overt cognitive impairment <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> .

text.text: These indicators capture different aspects of AD: APOE4 reflects inherited susceptibility, whereas Aβ burden provides a measure of underlying pathological processes.

Investigating their relationships with language therefore offers an opportunity to examine whether linguistic behavior contains information associated with both biological vulnerability and disease pathology at early stages.
Our central hypothesis is that different representations of language and cognition capture distinct, potentially complementary signals associated with these biological indicators.

In particular, we consider three sources of information: traditional cognitive assessment scores, which serve as our primary baseline; theory-driven (top-down) linguistic features extracted from spontaneous speech, which reflect the traditional approach to language analysis and serve as a second baseline; and language representations derived from pretrained LLMs.
These approaches characterize individuals from different perspectives.

Cognitive assessments measure performance on established neuropsychological tasks; predefined linguistic features capture specific aspects of language production and content; and LLM representations provide a broader, data-driven characterization of linguistic information.
Although all three may be informative about AD-related risk and pathology, there is no reason to assume that they capture the same information or succeed and fail on the same individuals.
We investigate this hypothesis using data from two longitudinal cohorts: the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention (WRAP) 27 and the Israel Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention (IRAP) 28 .
text.formatted: We investigate this hypothesis using data from two longitudinal cohorts: the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention (WRAP) <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> and the Israel Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention (IRAP) <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> .

text.text: Both cohorts include individuals at elevated risk for AD and provide cognitive assessments alongside genetic and neuroimaging information.
We analyze spontaneous speech elicited through the Cookie Theft task, using English-language data from WRAP and Hebrewlanguage data collected in IRAP specifically for this study.

The inclusion of these two cohorts allows us to examine the proposed approach across different languages and populations, while also extending computational language analysis to a Hebrew-speaking population that remains underrepresented in the AD literature [29] [30] [31].
text.formatted: The inclusion of these two cohorts allows us to examine the proposed approach across different languages and populations, while also extending computational language analysis to a Hebrew-speaking population that remains underrepresented in the AD literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: We develop separate predictive models based on each of the three sources of information using Hierarchical Multi-Domain Regression (HMDR), a linear modeling framework that estimates shared and domain-specific effects.

Importantly, rather than considering amyloid pathology only through a conventional positive-versus-negative distinction, we also examine multiple levels of amyloid accumulation, including levels below established clinical positivity thresholds.
This allows us to investigate whether the available linguistic and cognitive signals are informative about variation in Aβ burden during earlier stages of the pathological process.

We apply this approach to APOE4 carrier status and to global amyloid measures, and further extend the amyloid analysis to regional burden in the cingulate, frontal, parietal and temporal cortices to assess whether predictive patterns differ across brain regions.
Our results reveal that the three models achieve broadly comparable predictive performance, but their predictions differ substantially at the individual level.
Across tasks and cohorts, observations correctly classified by one model are frequently misclassified by another, and no single representation consistently dominates.
These findings provide evidence that the three sources of information capture complementary signals associated with APOE4 status and Aβ burden.
Motivated by this complementarity, we investigate whether the different signals can mutually enhance prediction.
We combine the three models using a simple ensemble that identifies a positive case whenever at least one constituent model predicts a positive outcome.

This ensemble is the best-performing model, significantly improving F1 relative to each individual model for both APOE4 and global amyloid in both cohorts, demonstrating the predictive value of integrating information from language and cognitive assessments.
The ensemble benefit also extends to regional amyloid outcomes, with significant advantages over all three constituent models in 21 of 24 tasks defined across the four cortical regions.

Together, these findings suggest that spontaneous language contains information associated with AD-related genetic risk and amyloid pathology that is not fully captured by standard . cognitive assessments.
They also demonstrate that theory-driven linguistic features and LLMbased representations provide complementary information, despite being derived from the same speech samples.

More broadly, our work provides evidence for the potential of combining modern language-based AI methods with established cognitive measures to improve the identification of biological indicators associated with early AD.
This offers a foundation for developing accessible, low-burden screening approaches and for enriching existing clinical assessments with computational analysis of spontaneous speech.

This study examined whether language-based representations capture signals associated with preclinical AD risk and pathology, and whether these signals can enhance traditional cognitive assessments.

We compared three sets of features: cognitive test scores, serving as the primary baseline for current clinical assessment; top-down, theory-driven linguistic features, representing the traditional approach to language analysis, and bottom-up linguistic embeddings derived from pretrained language models.
Three main findings emerged.
First, substantial individual-level disagreement among the constituent models indicated that each representation captured information not consistently recovered by the others.
Second, embedding-based representations generally performed best among the constituent models, although no single representation consistently outperformed the others across all tasks.

Third, combining the representations through an any-positive ensemble produced the best-performing model, significantly outperforming each constituent model and a prior-informed random baseline, and consistently yielding the highest F1 scores across both cohorts for APOE4 carrier status and global amyloid burden.

This advantage also extended to regional amyloid burden, with the ensemble significantly outperforming all three constituent models in 21 of the 24 regional prediction tasks across four brain regions.

Together, these findings suggest that linguistic representations and traditional cognitive measures capture complementary information associated with AD-related genetic risk and amyloid pathology, and that their integration improves predictive performance beyond that of individual representations.
This study provides a proof of concept for the potential utility of computational language analysis in preclinical AD research, with several implications for future clinical applications.

First, because the Cookie Theft picture-description task is already incorporated into many cognitive assessments, our approach could extract additional information from an existing assessment with minimal additional effort.
Second, language analysis could offer an accessible, low-burden screening approach to help identify individuals who may benefit from further clinical evaluation.
Third, repeated speech collection could enable more frequent monitoring of linguistic changes, potentially even in home-based settings.
This possibility is particularly relevant with the emergence of anti-amyloid treatments and the growing need for accessible methods of longitudinal monitoring.

Although the present study did not examine within-person changes or treatment response, it provides a foundation for investigating whether languagebased measures could serve as indicators of disease progression or response to treatment.

Importantly, the clinical use of such automated tools should be accompanied by healthcare professionals who can explain their clinical meaning and uncertainty, provide appropriate support, and guide individuals toward confirmatory assessment or available preventive and therapeutic options when indicated.
Language-based tools may therefore be most valuable as decision-support or screening instruments rather than as systems that communicate biological risk independently of clinical context.
This study shows consistent findings across two independent cohorts with substantially different linguistic and sociocultural characteristics.

This consistency is particularly meaningful given the predominance of English-speaking populations in research on speech and language markers of neurodegeneration 31 , alongside evidence that linguistic alterations associated with AD and MCI may vary across languages 17, [32] [33] [34] [35] .

Although differences in data collection and biomarker measurement complicate direct comparisons, the convergence of our central findings despite these provide strong evidence for their generalizability across diverse populations and settings.

Our findings add to growing evidence linking language characteristics to Aβ pathology in cognitively unimpaired and mildly impaired individuals 14, [36] [37] [38] [39] , including previous work in the WRAP cohort 37 .

text.text: Therefore, a key contribution of our study is the evaluation of amyloid burden across multiple distribution-based thresholds using LLM representations, rather than relying exclusively on a single clinical cutoff.

This approach is particularly relevant given growing evidence that Aβ accumulation below conventional positivity thresholds may precede more rapid biomarker progression and subtle cognitive changes [43] [44] [45] .

text.text: Our findings extend this evidence by suggesting that language-based representations capture signals associated with amyloid burden even below conventional thresholds for amyloid positivity.
Notably, disagreement in amyloid prediction was highest for the median-based classification tasks in both cohorts.

This pattern is consistent with the possibility that more pronounced amyloid-related patterns are captured more similarly across the three approaches, whereas subtler signals lead to more divergent predictions.

However, because median-based classification includes the full range of amyloid values and differs from quartile-based tasks in class balance, these findings do not establish that disagreement is concentrated specifically among individuals with intermediate amyloid burden.
Future analyses examining disagreement as a function of continuous amyloid burden could help clarify these patterns.
This work also contributes to the relatively limited literature on spontaneous speech and APOE4 carrier status.

text.text: By contrast, our study examines embeddingbased and top-down linguistic representations, capturing multiple dimensions of language, including lexical, syntactic, and content-related characteristics.
Beyond the range of linguistic dimensions represented, another strength of this study lies in the quality of the underlying transcripts and annotations.
Transcripts were carefully prepared by trained annotators following rigorous protocols.
The IRAP transcripts were produced and meticulously annotated specifically for the present research, rather than relying on pre-existing transcriptions or automated transcription alone.
This substantial data preparation effort involved independent annotation by two trained annotators, followed by adjudication of disagreements by a third annotator.

Unlike approaches relying on readily available transcripts or uncorrected Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) outputs, this procedure allowed careful preservation of subtle linguistic phenomena that may be particularly informative in preclinical AD research.
The same emphasis on quality extended to the extraction of top-down linguistic features, which combined manual, automated, and LLM-based approaches.

Disfluencies were manually annotated, an approach particularly valuable in clinical contexts, where subtle disruptions in speech may carry important signals of cognitive changes that off-the-shelf ASR systems may fail to capture reliably.

Lexical measures were computed using language-specific NLP tools and corpus-based frequency norms, while higher-level, theory-driven features were annotated . using a validated LLM-as-a-judge framework.
These procedures allowed us to preserve linguistic phenomena that could otherwise be lost during preprocessing and to examine their potential relevance to AD-related biological measures.
Importantly, the predictive linguistic signals identified in this study were obtained using relatively simple and computationally accessible approaches.
LLM embeddings were extracted from pretrained, off-the-shelf language models with frozen weights, without additional finetuning.
The top-down approach relied on only 13 theory-driven linguistic features, selected to represent diverse dimensions of language, including lexical, syntactic, and content-related characteristics.
Both representations were used as inputs to HMDR, a linear classifier.

Similarly, our ensemble employed a simple decision rule, classifying an observation as positive if at least one constituent model predicted a positive outcome, without additional training or parameter optimization.

The ability to combine lightweight approaches to predict AD-related indicators has important implications for future clinical applications, as their modest computational demands not only safeguard patient privacy through local deployment, but also ensure accessibility and reproducibility in resource-limited settings.

These results establish a foundation for further investigating the predictive value of spontaneous speech in preclinical AD, while demonstrating that meaningful signals can be extracted using relatively simple linguistic representations.
At the same time, the current approaches should not be considered an upper bound on achievable performance.

Future work could examine whether larger or task-adapted language models, fine-tuning with sufficiently large datasets, or broader sets of linguistically informed features provide additional predictive value.
Such developments should be evaluated against the interpretability, efficiency, and accessibility of the relatively lightweight approaches demonstrated here.
Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged.
First, although WRAP includes repeated speech observations for some participants, the present analyses do not model withinperson linguistic change over time.
Accordingly, the threshold-specific patterns cannot be interpreted as longitudinal trajectories of language change as Aβ accumulates.
Future repeatedmeasures analyses linking within-person changes in language and biomarkers are needed to test this directly.

Second, methodological and cohort-specific differences between IRAP and WRAP limit our ability to separate the observed associations between linguistic and cognitive measures and the target variables from potential influences of differences in data collection, biomarker measurement, and social and cultural characteristics.
IRAP and WRAP are active longitudinal cohorts whose protocols continue to evolve, creating differences in available measures and participant overlap across modalities.
We therefore focused on APOE4 and Aβ, the two ADrelated biological indicators currently available in both cohorts with sufficient overlap with Cookie Theft speech samples.
Other potentially informative markers are either available in only one cohort or do not yet have sufficient overlap with the speech data.
Particularly relevant future targets include tau and blood-based biomarkers such as GFAP and NfL, which are being collected as these cohorts continue to expand.

Although cognitive inputs were initially defined according to the established literature for each cohort, an additional evaluation using a harmonized set of cognitive measures available in both cohorts showed that the pattern remained largely unchanged, with no consistently superior constituent model and the ensemble outperforming all constituent models across tasks (Supplementary Methods 1.2 and Supplementary Tables 3 4 5).

Harmonizing amyloid . measures using Centiloid scaling, together with validation across additional languages and cohorts, could help disentangle these sources of variability.

Importantly, the consistency of these findings across two independent cohorts, despite linguistic, sociocultural, and methodological differences, further strengthens the evidence for the complementarity of linguistic and cognitive measures and the predictive benefits of integrated approaches.
Participants were drawn from two longitudinal cohorts focused on preclinical AD, IRAP and WRAP.
The cohorts comprised, respectively, middle-aged Hebrew-and English-speakers with a parental history of AD.
Available data included speech recordings, cognitive assessments, neuroimaging, genetic information, and electronic health records.
IRAP data were consolidated from several separate data files spanning June to September 2025; WRAP data were obtained from the November 30, 2025 data freeze.
All participants provided written informed consent.
Data collection was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Sheba Medical Center for IRAP and by the University of Wisconsin-Madison Institutional Review Board for WRAP.
To compare the language and cognitive models, we included observations for which both language and cognitive data were available, together with APOE4 carrier status, Aβ burden, or both.
The cognitive assessment and Cookie Theft task were typically completed on the same day.
However, these assessments could be separated in time from the Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scan used to quantify amyloid burden.
In both cohorts, PET scans were restricted to within ±8 years of the assessment, limiting the temporal gap while allowing to retain all available IRAP observations.
In both IRAP and WRAP cohorts, participants contributed speech samples across multiple visits.

For amyloid analyses, each speech sample was paired with the temporally closest eligible PET/PiB scan, allowing individual scans to serve multiple observations (IRAP: 59 observations across 58 unique scans; WRAP: 1,182 observations across 559 unique scans).

Because APOE4 genotype is time-invariant, single genotype calls were mapped across all repeated visits for each participant (IRAP: 126 observations from 125 unique calls; WRAP: 1,538 observations from 538 unique calls).
In IRAP, participants were classified using the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) 50 into Healthy Control (HC; n = 120) and MCI (n = 14) groups.

text.text: This process resulted in one of five classifications: Cognitively Unimpaired-Stable (CU-S; n=1,265), Cognitively Unimpaired-Declining (CU-D; n=222), MCI (n=46), impaired but not MCI (n=5), and dementia (n=3).

CU-S denotes individuals with normal cognition and no evidence of meaningful decline, whereas CU-D denotes individuals with evidence of cognitive decline that is not sufficient to meet criteria for MCI.

The impaired-but-not-MCI category includes individuals with cognitive impairment that was not classified as either CU-D or MCI, including cases in which impairment was considered longstanding rather than a decline from a previous level of functioning.

For cross-cohort comparison, cognitive status was harmonized into two categories: cognitively unimpaired (IRAP: HC; WRAP: CU-S and CU-D) and cognitively impaired (IRAP: MCI; WRAP: MCI, impaired but not MCI, and dementia).
APOE4 carrier status was treated as a binary classification task, defined as the presence of at least one ε4 allele of the APOE gene.
In both cohorts, APOE genotype information was obtained from blood samples.
Both cohorts used PET combined with Computed Tomography (PET-CT) scans to quantify amyloid tracer accumulation: the SUVR in IRAP, and PiB Index in WRAP.

To examine whether language and cognitive measures captured signals across different levels of amyloid accumulation, three binary classification tasks were defined separately for each cohort using cohort-specific thresholds: membership in the lowest quartile, values above the median, and membership in the highest quartile.
These tasks were defined for the global amyloid measure in each cohort and, separately, for each of four regional amyloid measures (cingulate, frontal, parietal, and temporal).
For the regional tasks, the thresholds were determined independently from the distribution of the corresponding region within each cohort, rather than reusing the global biomarker cutoffs.
Each cohort therefore contributed three global amyloid tasks and 12 regional amyloid tasks.

The embedding models spanned multilingual, English-specific, and Hebrew-specific architectures and varied in pretraining objectives, model size, and embedding dimensionality, as described in Supplementary Methods 2.1.

By incorporating both multilingual and language-specific architectures, this framework facilitates direct cross-cohort comparisons between English and Hebrew while maximizing representation quality within the Hebrew-speaking cohort.

In contrast to embedding-based representations, which encode text through latent semantic patterns that are not directly interpretable, the top-down approach relies on predefined, theorydriven features with explicit meaning, grounded in the clinical and linguistic literature.

text.text: These features assess the description as a whole rather than isolated words, sentences, or directly computed counts.

Developed in consultation with experts and grounded in previous dementia research, they characterize not only what information the speaker reports, but also how the speaker interprets and responds to the depicted situation.

Therefore, this approach complements conventional quantitative language measures by capturing complex, interpretable behaviors that are difficult to operationalize through simple counts or rule-based algorithms.
To enable these high-level features to be annotated at scale, we used Qwen3.5-9B 62 as the LLM annotator.

text.text: Model development for all classification tasks was conducted using stratified MCCV and HMDR, which captures shared population trends and domain-specific variations.
The HMDR formulation is detailed in Supplementary Methods 3.1.
In each iteration, 20% of the samples were randomly held out as an independent test set, while the remaining 80% were used for hyperparameter tuning.
All observations belonging to the same participant were assigned to the same partition.
In the APOE4 analyses, the feature vector contained either cognitive, embedding, or top-down features.
In amyloid-related tasks, both in IRAP and WRAP, the interval in years between the speech or cognitive assessment and the matched PET-CT scan was appended to the feature vector.
All features, including the scan-speech gap, were standardized within the training data before model fitting.

Hyperparameter selection was performed exclusively within the training set in two sequential phases (Supplementary Methods 3.2), each . using a separate stratified five-fold cross-validation procedure, with hyperparameters selected to maximize the positive-class F1 score.

Using F1 as the primary evaluation metric, we compare the constituent models with the anypositive ensemble to assess whether combining multiple representations yields a significant improvement in predictive performance.

As a reference for chance-level performance, all approaches were also compared with a prior-informed random baseline, which assigned class labels according to their proportions in the task's full sample.
The F1 score is defined as: (1) 𝐹1 = 2 × 𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛 × 𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙 𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛 + 𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙
Where: (2) 𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛 = 𝑇𝑃 𝑇𝑃 + 𝐹𝑃 (3) 𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙 = 𝑇𝑃 𝑇𝑃 + 𝐹𝑁 TP, FP, and FN denote true positives, false positives, and false negatives, respectively.
Precision, also known as Positive Predictive Value (PPV), measures how many of all cases predicted as positive are truly positive.
Recall, also known as sensitivity or True Positive Rate (TPR), measures how many of all actual positive cases are correctly identified by the model.
The F1 score combines precision and recall into a single measure, thereby accounting for both false-positive and false-negative errors.
By definition, it is their harmonic mean, therefore a low value for either precision or recall substantially reduces the overall F1 score.

text.text: Continuous demographic and clinical characteristics were summarized as mean (SD), and categorical variables as counts and percentages.

Differences between cohorts and between positive and negative outcome groups within each classification task were assessed using twosided Welch's t-tests for continuous variables and Pearson's chi-square tests for categorical variables.
Predictive performance was evaluated across 1,000 MCCV repetitions for APOE4 and global Aβ classification tasks, and 100 repetitions for regional Aβ tasks.
F1 scores were calculated separately for each outcome class on the held-out test sets and summarized as the mean across repetitions.
Mean F1 scores were reported with 95% confidence intervals.
Additional performance metrics included precision, recall, ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC (Supplementary Methods 3.3).
Pairwise comparisons of model performance were conducted using F1 scores obtained from matched MCCV test partitions.
For APOE4 and global Aβ tasks, comparisons proceeded in two stages.
First, the highest-performing constituent model was evaluated against the remaining two constituent models.

Second, the top-performing overall approach (consistently the "anypositive" ensemble in both tasks) was compared against the other four modeling approaches (the three constituent models and the prior-informed random baseline).

For regional Aβ tasks, only this second stage was conducted, comparing the best-performing approach with the remaining four approaches among the three constituent models, the ensemble, and the priorinformed random baseline.
Differences were assessed using two-sided paired t-tests, with BH .

FDR correction applied separately to the comparisons within each task and stage (two comparisons for constituent models, four for the full model comparison in APOE4, global Aβ, and regional Aβ tasks).
Full test statistics are reported in Supplementary Tables 6, 9, and 10.
Statistical significance was defined as q < 0.05.
